sources.outlet: Sandoval-Lentisco and Ioannidis, 'Cost of Retracted Articles to the NIH: a Living Analysis' (medRxiv preprint, on PMC)
sources.quote: The per-author cohort-wide median annual NIH funding fell from $133,293 in the 3 years pre-retraction to $55,973 in the 3 years post-retraction, a −58.0% change.
sources.searcher_note: Post-cutoff. NIH funding of all US authors with retractions, before and after retraction; not limited to ORI misconduct cases or to co-authors. Also: 26.7% of previously funded authors lost all NIH funding in the 3 years after first retraction.

sources.quote: Seventeen scientists found to have committed research misconduct during the last 25 years have since collectively received more than $101 million in NIH funding.
sources.searcher_note: Pattern: the ORI-sanctioned researchers themselves (not their co-authors) winning NIH money afterward; covers a study published 2017-02-01 in the Journal of Empirical Research on Human Research Ethics. Page shows no date.

sources.quote: Researchers experienced a median 91.8% decrease in publication output and large declines in funding after censure by the ORI.
sources.searcher_note: Earliest found: NIH money behind misconduct retractions ($58M, 1992-2012) and funding drop for ORI-censured researchers; the abstract does not cover co-authors.

notes: No source found counts co-authors of ORI-case retractions or the NIH money they won afterward; no hit on $187M. Closest pattern: sanctioned researchers themselves later won $101M (2017 study), and a July 2026 preprint on NIH funding of all retracted US authors. Science's news story on the $101M study ('U.S. researchers guilty of misconduct later won more than $100 million in NIH grants, study finds') returned 403, so the The Scientist copy is recorded instead. A 2019 Research Policy paper ('Guilt by association: How scientific misconduct harms prior collaborators') on citation penalties for collaborators of ORI-found scientists returned 403; its snippet says citations, not funding. A 2022 bioRxiv preprint (Ribeiro, Kalichman, Vasconcelos) on retractions and grant review had no counts in its abstract.
